summary: A note on socket number assignment. It warns of the danger of imposing more fixed socket number requirements on hosts and relates to RFCs 542, 503 and 451.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 617 warns protocol designers not to assume that every host can reserve socket numbers next to a Telnet socket. It recommends negotiating additional connections after the initial connection is established.

questions: why did rfc 617 argue against fixed socket numbers
subtitle: Why protocols should avoid assuming hosts can use fixed socket numbers.

tldr.problem: Protocols that assign data connections fixed socket numbers relative to a Telnet connection can conflict with how some host systems assign sockets to jobs and processes.
tldr.mechanism: The author argues that only initial connections need reserved socket conventions; protocols should negotiate later socket numbers over the existing Telnet connection.
tldr.outcome: The note warns that extra fixed-number requirements can exclude host software architectures or require awkward workarounds.

today: RFC 617 is a 1974 design note arguing against fixed socket-number assumptions beyond initial connection setup.

sections.title: Fixed Socket Numbers Can Limit Hosts
sections.content: The RFC notes that some protocols assume a user process can use a group of socket numbers around the Telnet sockets. It gives FTP's default data sockets and a proposed graphics connection as examples. The Host-Host Protocol, however, does not constrain host socket assignment apart from using the low-order bit to indicate data direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Some protocols expect a host to use socket numbers at fixed offsets from its Telnet connection. The author warns that hosts do not all assign sockets in the same way.

sections.title: The PDP-10 NCP Example
sections.content:
The RFC describes an NCP interface where programs could choose the low-order 8 bits and have the other 24 bits assigned by job, user or a guaranteed-unique allocation. A program could also specify all 32 bits under a stated ownership condition, if the resulting socket was not already in use.

In the described FTP server, control and data transfer ran in separate processes. Fixed offsets put data sockets in a range inaccessible to the data-transfer subjob, so the server had to open the data connections itself and reassign them to that subjob.
sections.plainLanguage: One host assigned socket numbers in ways that depended on jobs and users. Its FTP server had to use a workaround because fixed socket offsets did not fit its separate control and transfer processes.

sections.title: Negotiate Additional Connections
sections.content:
The author accepts that network-wide conventions are needed for initial connection, including reserving sockets 0–255 for standard ICP functions. He also considers it reasonable for a process to request a small block of adjacent sockets at once.

For later connections, he recommends exchanging socket numbers through negotiation over the existing Telnet connection. In his view, protocols should not specify fixed socket numbers beyond what is needed to establish the initial connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Initial connections can use agreed socket numbers. After that, the two sides should tell each other which sockets to use instead of relying on fixed offsets.
